questions.question: The chapter opens with 'Everything changes and nothing stands still.' Attribute it precisely.

options.text: Heraclitus of Ephesus, as quoted by Plato in Cratylus (360 BCE)
Plato, in The Republic (380 BCE)
Aristotle, in Metaphysics (350 BCE)
Parmenides, as quoted by Socrates (450 BCE)

questions.explanation: An epigraph about change rather than efficiency, because the chapter's real subject is evolvability: applications inevitably change over time.

questions.question: Which reasons does the chapter give for why applications change? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: New products are launched
User requirements become better understood
Business circumstances change
Hardware becomes cheaper

questions.explanation: It explicitly reconnects to the idea of evolvability introduced in Chapter 1 under 'Evolvability: Making Change Easy' on page 21.

questions.question: 'A change to an application's features also requires a change to data that it stores.' Which two shapes does this take? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A new field or record type needs to be captured
Existing data needs to be presented in a new way
Data needs to be moved to a different datacenter
Data needs to be encrypted

questions.explanation: Both are read-and-write shape changes, which is what makes encoding compatibility the chapter's subject.

questions.question: How do relational and schema-on-read databases differ in coping with a data-model change?

options.text: Relational databases generally assume all data conforms to one schema, changed by schema migrations, so there is exactly one schema in force at any one point in time. Schema-on-read ('schemaless') databases don't enforce a schema, so the database can contain a mixture of older and newer data formats written at different times
Both enforce exactly one schema at a time; they differ only in migration speed
Relational databases allow mixtures; schema-on-read databases enforce one schema
Neither has a schema, so the question doesn't arise

questions.explanation: 'Exactly one schema in force at any one point in time' is the precise phrase, and it is what migrations exist to preserve.

questions.question: Define the server-side deployment pattern the chapter names, and the benefits it claims.

options.text: A rolling upgrade, also called a staged rollout: deploying the new version to a few nodes at a time, checking whether it is running smoothly, and gradually working through all the nodes. This allows new versions to be deployed without service downtime, and thus encourages more frequent releases and better evolvability
A blue-green deployment: standing up a parallel cluster and switching traffic at once
A canary release: deploying to a test environment first
A big-bang deployment: upgrading all nodes simultaneously to avoid version skew

questions.explanation: The rolling upgrade is what forces old and new code to coexist, which is why compatibility matters.

questions.question: Why can't the client-side case be solved by a rolling upgrade?

options.text: Because with client-side applications you're at the mercy of the user, who may not install the update for some time
Because client code cannot be versioned
Because app stores forbid staged rollouts
Because clients have no persistent storage

questions.explanation: 'At the mercy of the user' is the chapter's exact phrase — there is no deployment mechanism that reaches an un-updated device.

questions.question: Write out the chapter's definitions of backward and forward compatibility. This is the most-often-inverted pair in the book.

options.text: Backward compatibility: newer code can read data that was written by older code. Forward compatibility: older code can read data that was written by newer code
Backward compatibility: older code can read data written by newer code. Forward compatibility: newer code can read data written by older code
Backward compatibility: data can be downgraded to an older schema. Forward compatibility: data can be upgraded to a newer schema
Backward compatibility: old clients can call new servers. Forward compatibility: new clients can call old servers

questions.explanation: The mnemonic in the names: backward looks back at old data; forward looks ahead to data from the future.

questions.question: Which direction is 'normally not hard' and which 'can be trickier', and why?

options.text: Backward compatibility is normally not hard: as the author of the newer code you know the format of data written by older code and can explicitly handle it, if necessary by simply keeping the old code around to read the old data. Forward compatibility can be trickier, because it requires older code to ignore additions made by a newer version of the code
Forward compatibility is normally not hard; backward compatibility is trickier because old formats are undocumented
Both are equally hard; the chapter draws no distinction
Backward compatibility is trickier because it requires rewriting data

questions.explanation: Asymmetry of knowledge: the new code can see the old format, but the old code cannot anticipate the new one.

questions.question: A node that hasn't been upgraded yet reads a record written by an already-upgraded node. Which compatibility property is at stake?

options.text: Backward compatibility
Forward compatibility
Neither — same-cluster reads are exempt
Both equally

questions.explanation: Older code reading newer data is forward compatibility. Conversely, new application code reading rows a five-year-old release wrote is backward compatibility — and storing something in the database is like sending a message to your future self, where backward compatibility is clearly necessary or your future self won't be able to decode what you previously wrote.

questions.question: Which encoding formats does the chapter say it will look at? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: JSON and XML
Protocol Buffers and Thrift
Avro
YAML and TOML

questions.explanation: For each it promises to say how they handle schema changes and how they support systems where old and new data and code need to coexist.

questions.question: Programs work with data in (at least) two representations. What are they, and what is each optimized for?

options.text: In memory: objects, structs, lists, arrays, hash tables, trees — optimized for efficient access and manipulation by the CPU, typically using pointers. On a file or network: a self-contained sequence of bytes, such as JSON — because a pointer wouldn't make sense to any other process
Compressed and uncompressed, optimized for space and speed respectively
Row-oriented and column-oriented, optimized for OLTP and OLAP
Encrypted and plaintext, optimized for security and performance

questions.explanation: 'Self-contained' is the load-bearing word: no external references may survive the boundary.

questions.question: The claim that the byte representation looks quite different from the in-memory one carries a footnote listing exceptions. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Certain memory-mapped files
When operating directly on compressed data, as described under Column Compression on page 97
When using shared memory between processes
When the data is smaller than one page

questions.explanation: Both are cases where the on-disk and in-memory layouts deliberately coincide.

questions.question: Name both directions of the translation with all their synonyms, and the footnote's disclaimer.

options.text: Encoding, also known as serialization or marshalling; and decoding, also known as parsing, deserialization or unmarshalling. The footnote notes that encoding has nothing to do with encryption, which the book does not discuss
Compression and decompression; the footnote notes compression is lossy
Packing and unpacking; the footnote notes packing is architecture-specific
Encryption and decryption; the footnote notes these are covered in Chapter 9

questions.explanation: Six words for two operations, plus an explicit disclaimer that this chapter is not about security.

questions.question: The chapter sets aside a box to justify one word choice. What is the clash?

options.text: 'Serialization' also has a completely different meaning in the context of transactions (Chapter 7), so to avoid overloading the word the book commits to 'encoding' — even though serialization is perhaps a more common term
'Encoding' clashes with character encoding, so the book uses 'serialization'
'Marshalling' clashes with a networking term, so the book uses 'parsing'
'Parsing' clashes with compiler terminology, so the book uses 'decoding'

questions.explanation: Serializability in transaction isolation is the conflicting meaning, and the concession — that serialization is the more common term — is part of the box.

questions.question: Which language-specific encoding facilities does the chapter cite? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: java.io.Serializable for Java, and the third-party library Kryo for Java
Marshal for Ruby
pickle for Python
JSON.stringify for JavaScript

questions.explanation: Many languages come with built-in support for encoding in-memory objects into byte sequences, and many third-party libraries also exist.

questions.question: What advantage does the chapter grant language built-in encoders, and what is the first 'deep problem'?

options.text: Advantage: they allow in-memory objects to be saved and restored with minimal additional code. Problem: the encoding is often tied to a particular programming language and reading the data in another language is very difficult — which means committing yourself to your current programming language for potentially a very long time, and precluding integrating your systems with those of other organizations
Advantage: they are the fastest available. Problem: they are not standardized
Advantage: they support schema evolution. Problem: they are verbose
Advantage: they are cross-language. Problem: they are insecure

questions.explanation: Convenience now, lock-in later — and the lock-in is both technical and organizational.

questions.question: Explain the security problem with language built-in serialization.

options.text: In order to restore data in the same object types, the decoding process needs to be able to instantiate arbitrary classes. If an attacker can get your application to decode an arbitrary byte sequence, they can instantiate arbitrary classes, which frequently allows them to do terrible things such as remotely executing arbitrary code
The encoding is plaintext, so data can be read in transit
The encoding includes memory addresses, leaking the heap layout
The encoding cannot be checksummed, so tampering is undetectable

questions.explanation: Arbitrary class instantiation is the mechanism; remote code execution is the consequence.

questions.question: Which are the remaining two problems, and which product does the chapter name and shame?

options.text: Versioning — because these libraries are designed for quick and easy encoding of data, they often neglect the inconvenient problems of forward and backward compatibility. And efficiency (CPU time to encode or decode, and the size of the encoded structure), also often an afterthought: Java's built-in serialization is notorious for its bad performance and bloated encoding
Portability and licensing; Python's pickle is named
Versioning and concurrency; Ruby's Marshal is named
Efficiency and durability; Kryo is named

questions.explanation: Four problems total: cross-language lock-in, security, versioning, efficiency.

questions.question: State the chapter's verdict on language built-ins, keeping its qualifier.

options.text: It's generally a bad idea to use your language's built-in encoding for anything other than very transient purposes
It is always wrong to use built-in encoding under any circumstances
Built-in encoding is preferred when both ends share a language
Built-in encoding is fine for durable storage but not for network transfer

questions.explanation: 'Anything other than very transient purposes' is the escape clause — and Akka is later named as a framework whose default is exactly this, to its cost.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the standing of JSON, XML and CSV?

options.text: They are widely known, widely supported, and almost as widely disliked. XML is often criticized for being too verbose and unnecessarily complicated; JSON's popularity is mainly due to its built-in support in web browsers (by virtue of being a subset of JavaScript) and its simplicity relative to XML; CSV is another popular language-independent format, albeit less powerful. All are textual formats and thus somewhat human-readable, although the syntax is a popular topic of debate
All three are universally admired; XML is praised for concision
JSON is popular because it is binary; CSV because it has a schema
All three are deprecated in favour of binary formats

questions.explanation: Note the hedge 'somewhat' on human-readability.

questions.question: The first subtle problem is numbers. What can XML and CSV not do, and what can JSON do and not do?

options.text: In XML and CSV you cannot distinguish between a number and a string that happens to consist of digits, except by referring to an external schema. JSON distinguishes strings and numbers, but it doesn't distinguish integers and floating-point numbers, and it doesn't specify a precision
XML distinguishes types natively; JSON cannot represent numbers at all
CSV distinguishes integers from floats; JSON does not distinguish strings from numbers
All three specify precision explicitly

questions.explanation: The precision gap is what causes the integer-overflow problem in JavaScript consumers.

questions.question: What is the exact integer boundary the chapter names, what causes it, and what workaround does Twitter use?

options.text: 2 to the 53rd power, which is 9,007,199,254,740,992 — the limit for integers that can be represented exactly in an IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point number, which is what JavaScript uses for all numbers. Twitter uses a 64-bit number to identify each tweet, and its API includes tweet IDs twice: once as a JSON number and once as a decimal string
2 to the 32nd power, caused by 32-bit integers; Twitter truncates IDs
2 to the 64th power, caused by unsigned integers; Twitter uses Base64
2 to the 31st power, caused by signed integers; Twitter uses a separate endpoint

questions.explanation: Sending the ID twice — once typed, once as a string — is a workaround for a consumer whose number type can't hold it.

questions.question: What do JSON and XML support and not support for binary data, and what is the exact size penalty of the workaround?

options.text: They have good support for Unicode character strings but don't support binary strings (sequences of bytes without a character encoding). People get around this by encoding the binary data as text using Base64, with the schema used to indicate that the value should be interpreted as Base64-encoded — a hacky workaround that increases the data size by 33%, because Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters
They support binary natively, so no workaround is needed
They use hex encoding, which doubles the data size
They use URL encoding, which increases size by 200%

questions.explanation: 4 characters per 3 bytes is a ratio of 4/3, hence the 33% overhead.

questions.question: State the chapter's position on XML and JSON schema support.

options.text: There is optional schema support for both. These schema languages are quite powerful, and thus quite complicated to learn and implement. Use of XML schemas is fairly widespread, but many JSON-based tools don't bother using schemas — so applications that use such formats have to hardcode the appropriate encoding and decoding logic instead
Both mandate schemas, so all tools use them
Neither has any schema support
JSON schemas are widespread; XML schemas do not exist

questions.explanation: Optional plus complicated equals widely skipped — and the logic moves into application code.

questions.question: Which complaints are specific to CSV? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It does not have any schema, so it is up to the application to define the meaning of each row and column
If an application change adds a new row or column, you have to handle that change manually
It is a quite vague format — what happens if a value contains a comma or a newline character? Although its escaping rules have been formally specified, not all parsers implement them correctly
It cannot represent numbers at all

questions.explanation: The escaping rules are RFC 4180, and the complaint is about implementations, not the specification.

questions.question: In what role does the chapter predict textual formats will remain popular, and what is its decisive argument?

options.text: Especially as data interchange formats — sending data from one organization to another. The decisive argument: the difficulty of getting different organizations to agree on anything outweighs most other concerns, so as long as people agree on what the format is, it often doesn't matter how pretty or efficient the format is
Especially for internal storage, because parsing speed dominates
Especially for logs, because they must be human-readable
They will not remain popular; binary formats will replace them

questions.explanation: Coordination cost, not technical merit, is what keeps these formats alive.

questions.question: When does the pressure to use a lowest-common-denominator format disappear, and at what scale does the choice start to matter?

options.text: For data used only internally within your organization there is less pressure to use a lowest-common-denominator encoding format, so you can choose something more compact or faster to parse. For a small dataset the gains are negligible, but once you get into the terabytes the choice of data format can have a big impact
The pressure disappears once you exceed a gigabyte, regardless of audience
The pressure never disappears, since all data eventually leaves the organization
The pressure disappears for public APIs, where efficiency matters most

questions.explanation: Audience determines the constraint; volume determines whether it's worth paying to relax it.

questions.question: Name the binary variants of JSON and XML the chapter lists, and their collective fate. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For JSON: MessagePack, BSON, BJSON, UBJSON, BISON and Smile
For XML: WBXML and Fast Infoset
Some have been adopted in various niches, but none of them are as widely adopted as the textual versions of JSON and XML
All of them have displaced the textual versions in practice

questions.explanation: JSON is less verbose than XML, but both still use a lot of space compared to binary formats — which is what motivated the variants.

questions.question: What is the fatal limitation shared by all these binary variants?

options.text: Some extend the set of datatypes (for example distinguishing integers and floating-point numbers, or adding support for binary strings) but they keep the JSON/XML data model unchanged. In particular, since they don't prescribe a schema, they need to include all the object field names within the encoded data — so strings like userName, favoriteNumber and interests are repeated in every record
They cannot represent nested objects
They are not human-readable, which is their only drawback
They drop support for arrays

questions.explanation: Carrying field names in the data is exactly the cost that schema-driven formats eliminate.

questions.question: In the MessagePack encoding of the example record, what does the first byte 0x83 mean?

options.text: That what follows is an object (top four bits 0x80) with three fields (bottom four bits 0x03)
That what follows is a string of length 3
That the record uses schema version 3
That there are 83 bytes to follow

questions.explanation: The second byte, 0xa8, indicates a string (top four bits 0xa0) that is eight bytes long (bottom four bits 0x08) — the eight bytes that follow spell userName in ASCII, with no need for any marker to tell us where the string ends. The next seven bytes encode the six-letter value Martin with a prefix 0xa6.

questions.question: Packing the field count into four bits allows only 0 to 15. What happens with more than 15 fields?

options.text: A different type indicator is used, and the number of fields is encoded in two or four bytes
The record is rejected as invalid
The object is split into two objects
Field names are dropped to save space

questions.explanation: The compact form is an optimization for the common case, with an escape hatch for larger objects.

questions.question: What are the byte counts for the example record in textual JSON and in MessagePack, and what verdict does the chapter draw?

options.text: 81 bytes with whitespace removed, versus 66 bytes for MessagePack — a saving of 15 bytes, about 18.5%. The chapter's verdict: it is not clear whether such a small space reduction is worth the loss of human-readability
81 bytes versus 32 bytes, a decisive win for MessagePack
100 bytes versus 66 bytes, a clear win worth the readability loss
66 bytes versus 81 bytes — MessagePack is larger

questions.explanation: The chapter immediately promises better, which is what the schema-driven formats deliver.

questions.question: Give the provenance of Thrift and Protocol Buffers.

options.text: Apache Thrift and Protocol Buffers (protobuf) are binary encoding libraries based on the same principle; Protocol Buffers was originally developed at Google and Thrift at Facebook, and both were made open source in 2007–08
Thrift at Google and protobuf at Facebook, both open sourced in 2005
Both at Apache, open sourced in 2010
Thrift at Twitter and protobuf at LinkedIn, open sourced in 2009

questions.explanation: Both require a schema for any data that is encoded — the defining difference from the binary JSON variants.

questions.question: In the Thrift interface definition language, what do the numbers 1:, 2:, 3: declare?

options.text: Field tags — compact aliases for fields, so the field name need not be spelled out in the encoded data
The order in which fields must be written
The byte offsets of each field
Schema version numbers for each field

questions.explanation: Thrift's schema also marks each field required or optional and gives its type, including a dedicated parameterized list datatype and an i64 for 64-bit integers.

questions.question: Which differences does the chapter name between the Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas for the same record? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Protobuf uses the keyword message rather than struct, and writes field tags as '= 1' rather than '1:'
Protobuf spells the type int64 and uses snake_case field names such as user_name and favorite_number
Where Thrift has a parameterized list datatype, protobuf marks the field 'repeated' — a third option alongside required and optional
Protobuf has no field tags at all

questions.explanation: The chapter calls the two schemas very similar; the repeated marker is the one structural divergence.

questions.question: What tooling do Thrift and Protocol Buffers ship with, and what does your code do with the output?

options.text: A code generation tool that takes a schema definition and produces classes implementing the schema in various programming languages; your application code can call this generated code to encode or decode records of the schema
A schema registry that must be queried at runtime
An interpreter that reads the schema at runtime, with no code generation
A migration tool that rewrites stored data

questions.explanation: Code generation is what makes these formats convenient in statically typed languages and awkward in dynamic ones.

questions.question: The body text says Thrift has two binary encoding formats. What does the footnote correct?

options.text: There are actually three: BinaryProtocol, CompactProtocol, and DenseProtocol — but DenseProtocol is only supported by the C++ implementation, so it doesn't count as cross-language. Thrift also has two different JSON-based encoding formats, for five encodings in total
There is only one, BinaryProtocol
There are four, all cross-language
The footnote confirms there are exactly two

questions.explanation: The footnote ends with 'What fun!' — three binary (one non-cross-language) plus two JSON-based.

questions.question: How many bytes does Thrift's BinaryProtocol take for the example record, and what annotations does each field carry?

options.text: 59 bytes. Each field gets a type annotation indicating whether it is a string, integer or list, and where required a length indication — with four-byte lengths and a full eight bytes for the number 1337. String values are encoded as ASCII (or rather, UTF-8)
34 bytes, with only a type annotation per field
66 bytes, with field names inline
33 bytes, with variable-length integers

questions.explanation: The strings Martin, daydreaming and hacking are encoded as UTF-8, similar to MessagePack.

questions.question: What is 'the big difference' between Thrift's BinaryProtocol encoding and MessagePack's?

options.text: There are no field names — instead the encoded data contains field tags, the numbers 1, 2 and 3 from the schema definition. Field tags are like aliases for fields: a compact way of saying what field we're talking about without having to spell out the field name
There are no type annotations
Strings are compressed rather than stored raw
The record has no length prefix

questions.explanation: Replacing names with numbers is the entire space saving — and it is why tags may never be reassigned.

questions.question: Thrift's CompactProtocol encodes the same record in 34 bytes. Which techniques shrink it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Packing the field type and tag number into a single byte
Using variable-length integers, so the number 1337 takes two bytes rather than a full eight, with the top bit of each byte used to indicate whether there are still more bytes to come
Dropping the type annotations entirely
Compressing the string values with gzip

questions.explanation: CompactProtocol is semantically equivalent to BinaryProtocol — 25 bytes saved with no change in meaning.

questions.question: Which variable-length integer ranges does the chapter state?

options.text: Numbers between –64 and 63 are encoded in one byte; numbers between –8192 and 8191 in two bytes; bigger numbers use more bytes
Numbers between 0 and 255 in one byte; 0 and 65535 in two bytes
Numbers between –128 and 127 in one byte; –32768 and 32767 in two bytes
All integers take exactly four bytes

questions.explanation: The top bit of each byte is a continuation flag, leaving 7 payload bits per byte — so one byte carries 7 signed bits (–64 to 63) and two bytes carry 14 (–8192 to 8191).

questions.question: How does Protocol Buffers' encoding of the example record compare?

options.text: Protobuf has only one binary encoding format and does the bit packing slightly differently, but is otherwise very similar to Thrift's CompactProtocol; it takes 33 bytes, one fewer, with two repetitions of tag 3 for the list and no end-of-struct byte
Protobuf takes 59 bytes, like Thrift's BinaryProtocol
Protobuf takes 66 bytes, like MessagePack
Protobuf has three binary formats and takes 34 bytes in the most compact

questions.explanation: 33 versus 34 bytes — essentially a tie with Thrift's CompactProtocol.

questions.question: What do the required and optional markers actually buy?

options.text: Nothing in the encoding — the marker makes no difference to how the field is encoded, and nothing in the binary data indicates whether a field was required. The difference is simply that required enables a runtime check that fails if the field is not set, which can be useful for catching bugs
Required fields are encoded without a tag, saving a byte
Required fields are written first in the byte stream
Required fields are validated by the schema registry at write time

questions.explanation: Which is why a required field can never be safely removed: it is a runtime assertion, not an encoding feature.

questions.question: Define schema evolution, and state what you may rename versus what you may never change.

options.text: Schema evolution is the fact that schemas inevitably need to change over time. An encoded record is just the concatenation of its encoded fields, each identified by its tag number and annotated with a datatype; if a field value is not set it is simply omitted. You can change the name of a field in the schema, since the encoded data never refers to field names — but you cannot change a field's tag, since that would make all existing encoded data invalid
You may change tags but never names
You may change both freely
You may change neither

questions.explanation: Tags are the identity of a field; names are only documentation.

questions.question: How does adding a field preserve compatibility, and by what mechanism?

options.text: You give the new field a new tag number. If old code tries to read data written by new code, including a tag it doesn't recognize, it can simply ignore that field — the datatype annotation allows the parser to determine how many bytes it needs to skip. This maintains forward compatibility: old code can read records written by new code
It maintains backward compatibility, because new code can skip old fields
It maintains neither; adding a field is always breaking
It maintains forward compatibility because old code rejects unknown tags

questions.explanation: Skippability via the type annotation is the mechanism that makes unknown fields harmless.

questions.question: What makes new code able to read old data, and what is the 'only detail' you must respect?

options.text: As long as each field has a unique tag number, new code can always read old data because the tag numbers still have the same meaning. The only detail: if you add a new field you cannot make it required, since that check would fail if new code read data written by old code, which would not have written the new field. So every field you add after the initial deployment of the schema must be optional or have a default value
New fields must be required, so that old data is rejected
New fields must reuse an existing tag number
New code must be given the old schema at runtime

questions.explanation: The required marker is a runtime assertion, which is precisely why it cannot be applied retroactively.

questions.question: Which rules apply to removing a field? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Removing a field is just like adding a field, with backward and forward compatibility concerns reversed
You can only remove a field that is optional — a required field can never be removed
You can never use the same tag number again, because you may still have data written somewhere that includes the old tag number, and that field must be ignored by new code
You must also rename the field to mark it deprecated

questions.explanation: Tag numbers are permanently burned once used, which is why long-lived schemas accumulate reserved tags.

questions.question: You widen a field from a 32-bit to a 64-bit integer. What happens in each direction?

options.text: Changing the datatype may be possible — check the documentation — but there is a risk that values will lose precision or get truncated. New code reading old data is fine: the parser can fill in any missing bits with zeros. Old code reading new data is the problem: the old code is still using a 32-bit variable, so if the decoded 64-bit value won't fit in 32 bits it will be truncated
Both directions are always safe, since integers are variable-length
New code reading old data truncates; old code reading new data is safe
Neither direction works; you must add a new field

questions.explanation: Widening is forward-incompatible: the old reader's variable is too narrow for what the new writer may produce.

questions.question: Protocol Buffers has no list datatype. How does repeated work, and what evolution does it enable?

options.text: The repeated marker means just what it says on the tin: the same field tag simply appears multiple times in the record. This makes it okay to change an optional single-valued field into a repeated multi-valued field — new code reading old data sees a list with zero or one elements, and old code reading new data sees only the last element of the list. Thrift's dedicated parameterized list datatype does not allow this evolution, but does have the advantage of supporting nested lists
repeated stores a length prefix, and the evolution is not possible
repeated is identical to Thrift's list in every respect
repeated only works for strings, not for other types

questions.explanation: Repetition-as-a-list buys single-to-multi evolution at the cost of nesting.

questions.question: Give Avro's origin story.

options.text: Apache Avro is another binary encoding format that is interestingly different from Protocol Buffers and Thrift; it was started in 2009 as a subproject of Hadoop, as a result of Thrift not being a good fit for Hadoop's use cases
Avro was started at Google in 2007 as a protobuf successor
Avro was started in 2009 at Facebook as a Thrift successor
Avro was standardized in 1984 as part of ASN.1

questions.explanation: Hadoop's need for dynamically generated schemas is what drove Avro's distinctive design.

questions.question: Avro has two schema languages. What are they for?

options.text: Avro IDL, intended for human editing, and one based on JSON that is more easily machine-readable
One for reading and one for writing
One for statically typed and one for dynamically typed languages
One for records and one for unions

questions.explanation: Human-editable versus machine-readable, expressing exactly the same schemas.

questions.question: What is most notable about the Avro IDL schema compared with the Thrift and protobuf versions?

options.text: There are no tag numbers anywhere in the schema. It declares a record with a string field, a union of null and long with a default of null, and an array of string — but no field tags
It has tag numbers but no datatypes
It has no field names, only tags
It requires every field to be marked required

questions.explanation: The absence of tag numbers is the root of Avro's differences: resolution is by field name instead. In the JSON form, the union becomes a JSON array of type names, the default is an explicit 'default: null' key, and the array's element type is a nested 'items: string'.

questions.question: How many bytes does Avro take for the example record, and how does it rank?

options.text: Just 32 bytes — the most compact of all the encodings the chapter has shown
33 bytes, tied with Protocol Buffers
34 bytes, tied with Thrift CompactProtocol
59 bytes, the least compact binary format

questions.explanation: About a 60% reduction from the 81-byte textual JSON, and the smallest of the set.

questions.question: How does a reader parse Avro data, and what does that seem to imply?

options.text: There is nothing to identify fields or their datatypes in the byte sequence — it simply consists of values concatenated together, so you go through the fields in the order they appear in the schema and use the schema to tell you the datatype of each field. This implies the data can only be decoded correctly if the code reading the data is using the exact same schema as the code that wrote it — any mismatch would mean incorrectly decoded data. The chapter immediately qualifies this: the schemas need only be compatible
Each value carries a tag and type, read in any order
The reader scans for field names embedded in the data
The reader must have the writer's exact schema with no exceptions

questions.explanation: The strict-looking consequence is the setup for the writer's-schema / reader's-schema distinction that relaxes it.

questions.question: Define the writer's schema and the reader's schema.

options.text: The writer's schema is whatever version of the schema the application encoding the data knows about — it may be compiled into the application. The reader's schema is the schema the application decoding the data is expecting the data to be in, which the application code is relying on and which may have been generated from that schema during the build process
The writer's schema is stored in the database; the reader's schema is negotiated at runtime
They are the same thing viewed from two sides
The writer's schema is the newest version; the reader's is the oldest

questions.explanation: Two independently-versioned artifacts, which is what makes resolution necessary.

questions.question: State 'the key idea with Avro' and the mechanism that implements it.

options.text: The writer's schema and the reader's schema don't have to be the same — they only need to be compatible. When data is decoded, the Avro library resolves the differences by looking at the writer's schema and the reader's schema side by side and translating the data from the writer's schema into the reader's schema. The Avro specification defines exactly how this resolution works
Both schemas must be byte-identical, verified by hash
The reader always upgrades the data to the newest schema before decoding
The writer embeds both schemas in every record

questions.explanation: Figure 4-6 depicts an Avro reader resolving differences between the writer's schema and the reader's schema.

questions.question: Which schema-resolution rules does Avro define? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It's no problem if the writer's and reader's schemas have their fields in a different order, because schema resolution matches up the fields by field name
If the code reading the data encounters a field that appears in the writer's schema but not in the reader's schema, it is ignored
If the code reading the data expects some field but the writer's schema does not contain a field of that name, it is filled in with a default value declared in the reader's schema
If field types differ, the reader raises an error and stops

questions.explanation: Matching by name rather than by tag is what makes order irrelevant — the property Avro gets from having no tag numbers.

questions.question: Restate forward and backward compatibility in Avro's writer/reader vocabulary.

options.text: Forward compatibility means you can have a new version of the schema as writer and an old version as reader; backward compatibility means you can have a new version as reader and an old version as writer
Forward compatibility means a new reader with an old writer; backward means a new writer with an old reader
Both mean the reader must be newer than the writer
Both mean the writer must be newer than the reader

questions.explanation: So in the forward case the reader is old, and in the backward case the reader is new — the classic point of confusion.

questions.question: State the single Avro evolution rule.

options.text: To maintain compatibility, you may only add or remove a field that has a default value. The favoriteNumber field in the example schema has a default value of null, so if you add a field with a default value and a reader using the new schema reads a record written with the old schema, the default value is filled in for the missing field
You may only add fields, never remove them
You may add or remove any field, since matching is by name
You may only change fields that are in a union type

questions.explanation: One rule covers both directions, in contrast to Thrift/protobuf's separate rules for required and optional.

questions.question: Which mistake breaks which compatibility direction in Avro?

options.text: Adding a field that has no default value breaks backward compatibility, because new readers wouldn't be able to read data written by old writers. Removing a field that has no default value breaks forward compatibility, because old readers wouldn't be able to read data written by new writers
Adding breaks forward compatibility; removing breaks backward compatibility
Both mistakes break backward compatibility only
Neither breaks compatibility, because of name matching

questions.explanation: Add breaks backward; remove breaks forward. A favourite exam inversion.

questions.question: How does Avro treat null, and what is the restriction?

options.text: In many programming languages null is an acceptable default for any variable, but this is not the case in Avro: to allow a field to be null you have to use a union type, for example a union of null, long and string, meaning the field can be a number, a string, or null. You can only use null as a default value if it is one of the branches of the union. A footnote adds the extra precision that the default value must be of the type of the first branch of the union — a specific limitation of Avro, not a general feature of union types
null is a valid default for every field, as in most languages
null is forbidden entirely in Avro schemas
null requires a separate nullable marker on each field

questions.explanation: The chapter says this verbosity helps prevent bugs by being explicit about what can and cannot be null, citing Tony Hoare's 'Null References: The Billion Dollar Mistake'.

questions.question: What does Avro have instead of required and optional markers?

options.text: Union types and default values — Avro doesn't have optional and required markers in the same way as Protocol Buffers and Thrift do
Field tags with presence bits
A nullable keyword on each field
Nothing; all Avro fields are required

questions.explanation: Note the careful hedge 'in the same way' — the capability exists, expressed differently.

questions.question: Give Avro's rules for changing a field's datatype, its name, and adding a union branch.

options.text: Changing the datatype is possible provided that Avro can convert the type. Changing a field name is possible — the reader's schema can contain aliases for field names, so it can match an old writer's schema field name against the aliases — which makes changing a field name backward compatible but not forward compatible. Similarly, adding a branch to a union type is backward compatible but not forward compatible
All three changes are both backward and forward compatible
Renaming and adding a union branch are forward compatible but not backward compatible
None of the three changes is possible in Avro

questions.explanation: Aliases are read by the reader, so only the reader-is-new direction works — hence backward but not forward.

questions.question: Why can't you just ship the schema with each record?

options.text: Because the schema would likely be much bigger than the encoded data, making all the space savings from the binary encoding futile
Because schemas cannot be serialized
Because the reader cannot parse a schema at runtime
Because Avro forbids it in the specification

questions.explanation: The glossed-over question is: how does the reader know the writer's schema with which a particular piece of data was encoded?

questions.question: How does the reader obtain the writer's schema in each of the three contexts? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Large file with lots of records — a common Hadoop use case is a file containing millions of records all encoded with the same schema, so the writer's schema is included once at the beginning of the file. Avro specifies a file format (object container files) to do this

Database with individually written records — different records may be written at different points in time with different writer's schemas, so you include a version number at the beginning of every encoded record and keep a list of schema versions in your database; a reader fetches the writer's schema for that version number. LinkedIn's Espresso works this way

Sending records over a network connection — two processes communicating over a bidirectional network connection can negotiate the schema version on connection setup and use that schema for the lifetime of the connection, as the Avro RPC protocol does
Broadcast to unknown recipients — the schema is published to DNS

questions.explanation: Object container files are discussed further in Chapter 10.

questions.question: Beyond decoding, what does a database of schema versions give you?

options.text: It acts as documentation, and it gives you a chance to check schema compatibility. The version number could be a simple incrementing integer, or a hash of the schema
It enables automatic data migration
It provides encryption key rotation
It allows schemas to be deleted safely

questions.explanation: A schema registry is a useful thing to have in any case, independent of the decoding requirement.

questions.question: What advantage does Avro's lack of tag numbers give with a relational-database dump?

options.text: Avro is friendlier to dynamically generated schemas. You generate a record schema for each database table, where each column becomes a field in that record and the column name maps to the field name in Avro, then dump it all to an Avro object container file. If the database schema changes, you can just generate a new Avro schema from the updated database schema and export data in the new schema — the data export process does not need to pay any attention to the schema change, because the fields are identified by name
Avro can infer the schema at read time with no schema at all
Avro stores column names in every record, so schemas are unnecessary
Avro requires manual tag assignment, which makes dumps reproducible

questions.explanation: Name-based resolution means a regenerated schema just works, with no tag bookkeeping.

questions.question: What would you have to do instead with Thrift or Protocol Buffers?

options.text: The field tags would likely have to be assigned by hand: every time the database schema changes, an administrator would have to manually update the mapping from database column names to field tags. It would be possible to automate this, but the schema generator would have to be very careful not to assign previously used field tags. This kind of dynamically generated schema simply wasn't a design goal of Thrift or Protocol Buffers, whereas it was for Avro
Nothing different — both handle generated schemas identically
You would have to disable tag checking
You would have to convert the dump to JSON first

questions.explanation: The difference is one of design intent, not just capability.

questions.question: What does code generation bring in statically typed languages, and why is it pointless or harmful in dynamically typed ones? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In statically typed languages like Java, C++ and C# it allows efficient in-memory structures to be used for decoded data, and allows type checking and autocompletion in IDEs when writing programs that access the data structures
In dynamically typed languages like JavaScript, Ruby and Python there is not much point in generating code, since there is no compile-time type checker to satisfy

Code generation is often frowned upon in these languages since they otherwise avoid an explicit compilation step, and with a dynamically generated schema code generation is an unnecessary obstacle to getting to the data
Code generation is required in all languages for Avro to work

questions.explanation: Which is why Avro offers optional code generation.

questions.question: What makes it possible to use Avro without code generation?

options.text: The object container file embeds the writer's schema, so it is self-describing: you can simply open it with a library that supports Avro and look at the data in the same way as you could look at a JSON file, because the file includes all the necessary metadata. This makes tools like Apache Pig possible — you can open some Avro files, start analyzing them, and write derived datasets to output files in Avro format without even thinking about schemas
Avro data carries field names inline in every record
Avro can guess the schema from the byte pattern
Avro requires the reader's schema to be registered in advance

questions.explanation: Self-description at the file level, not the record level, is what gives Avro its dynamic ergonomics.

questions.question: How do the schema languages of Protocol Buffers, Thrift and Avro compare to XML Schema and JSON Schema?

options.text: They are much simpler, since XML Schema and JSON Schema support much more detailed validation rules — for example that the string value of a field must match a regular expression, or that the integer value of a field must be between 0 and 100. As these formats are simpler, they are simpler to implement and simpler to use, and they support a fairly wide range of programming languages
They are more complex, supporting richer validation
They are equivalent in expressiveness
They support no validation at all, unlike XML Schema

questions.explanation: Less validation power, more implementations and easier adoption.

questions.question: Give the full case the chapter makes about ASN.1.

options.text: ASN.1 is a schema definition language first standardized in 1984, used to define various network protocols; its binary encoding DER is still used to encode SSL certificates (X.509). It supports schema evolution using tag numbers, similar to Protocol Buffers and Thrift. However, it's also very complex and badly documented, so ASN.1 is probably not a good choice for new applications
ASN.1 dates from 1994 and is no longer used anywhere
ASN.1 uses name-based resolution like Avro and is recommended for new work
ASN.1 is a textual format superseded by XML

questions.explanation: The ideas on which these encodings are based are by no means new — ASN.1 predates them by over two decades.

questions.question: What other family of binary encodings does the chapter point at, and what hides it from you?

options.text: Proprietary ones: most relational databases have a network protocol over which you can send queries and get responses, generally specific to a particular database, and the vendor provides a driver (for example using the ODBC or JDBC APIs) that decodes responses from the database's network protocol into in-memory data structures
Filesystem formats, hidden by the operating system
CPU instruction encodings, hidden by the compiler
TLS record formats, hidden by the network stack

questions.explanation: The driver is the abstraction that keeps a proprietary wire format invisible.

questions.question: Which advantages of schema-driven binary encodings does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They can be much more compact than the various binary JSON variants, since they can omit field names from the encoded data
The schema is a valuable form of documentation, and because the schema is required for decoding you can be sure it is up to date (unlike manually maintained documentation, which easily drifts)
Keeping a database of schemas allows you to check forward and backward compatibility of schema changes before anything is deployed
For users of statically typed programming languages, the ability to generate code from the schema enables type checking at compile time

questions.explanation: Four properties — most readers remember only compactness and code generation.

questions.question: State the chapter's closing claim about schema evolution versus schemaless databases.

options.text: Although textual data formats such as JSON, XML and CSV are widespread, binary encodings based on schemas are also a viable option: schema evolution allows the same kind of flexibility as schemaless / schema-on-read JSON databases provide, while also providing better guarantees about your data and better tooling
Binary encodings are better in all cases and textual formats should be abandoned
Schemaless databases provide strictly more flexibility than schema evolution
Schema evolution is only useful for analytics workloads

questions.explanation: The claim is 'also a viable option', not 'better in all cases' — and the flexibility claim is matched, not exceeded.

questions.question: How does the chapter define what compatibility actually is?

options.text: Compatibility is a relationship between one process that encodes the data and another process that decodes it — which is why the organizing question becomes: who encodes the data, and who decodes it?
Compatibility is a property of a single schema version
Compatibility is a property of the encoding library
Compatibility is a property of the deployment process

questions.explanation: Framing it as a relationship is what leads to the three dataflow modes: databases (page 129), service calls (page 131), and asynchronous message passing (page 136).

questions.question: In a database, who encodes and who decodes, and what is the memorable phrase for the single-process case?

options.text: The process that writes to the database encodes the data and the process that reads from it decodes it. There may just be a single process accessing the database, in which case the reader is simply a later version of the same process — and you can think of storing something in the database as sending a message to your future self. Backward compatibility is clearly necessary here; otherwise your future self won't be able to decode what you previously wrote
The database encodes and the application decodes; forward compatibility is necessary
The reader encodes and the writer decodes; neither compatibility is needed
The driver encodes and the storage engine decodes; only forward compatibility matters

questions.explanation: Writing to storage is communication with your future self.

questions.question: Why is forward compatibility 'also often required for databases'?

options.text: Because it's common for several different processes to be accessing a database at the same time — several different applications or services, or simply several instances of the same service for scalability or fault tolerance. That means some processes accessing the database will be running newer code and some older code, for example because a new version is currently being deployed in a rolling upgrade: a value may be written by a newer version of the code and subsequently read by an older version
Because databases replicate data to older replicas
Because backups are restored into older versions
It is not required; only backward compatibility matters for databases

questions.explanation: Rolling upgrades put old and new readers on the same data at the same time.

questions.question: Describe 'an additional snag' with database dataflow.

options.text: You add a field to a record schema and newer code writes a value for that new field to the database; subsequently an older version of the code, which doesn't yet know about the new field, reads the record, updates it, and writes it back. The desirable behaviour is for the old code to keep the new field intact, even though it couldn't be interpreted — otherwise, when an older version of the application updates data previously written by a newer version, data may be lost
Old code crashes on encountering an unknown field
The database rejects the write from old code
The new field is silently renamed

questions.explanation: Read-modify-write by an old reader is the specific path that loses data, which is what Figure 4-7 depicts.

questions.question: Where does the risk of losing unknown fields actually live, and how hard is it to solve?

options.text: The encoding formats support such preservation of unknown fields, but sometimes you need to take care at an application level: if you decode a database value into model objects in the application and later reencode those model objects, the unknown field might be lost in that translation process. Solving this is not a hard problem; you just need to be aware of it
The risk lives in the encoding format and cannot be solved
The risk lives in the database engine and requires a schema registry
The risk lives in the network layer and requires idempotent writes

questions.explanation: The format preserves the field; the application's object mapping is where it gets dropped.

questions.question: What illustration does the chapter give of how wide the age spread of values in one database can be?

options.text: Because a database generally allows any value to be updated at any time, within a single database you may have some values that were written five milliseconds ago and some that were written five years ago
Values are all rewritten nightly, so the spread is at most one day
Values expire after 90 days, bounding the spread
The spread is bounded by the replication lag

questions.explanation: Five milliseconds to five years, in the same table.

questions.question: Contrast the timescale of replacing application code with that of database contents, and give the slogan.

options.text: When you deploy a new version of your application — of a server-side application, at least — you may entirely replace the old version with the new version within a few minutes. The same is not true of database contents: five-year-old data will still be there, in the original encoding, unless you have explicitly rewritten it since then. This is sometimes summed up as data outlives code
Code outlives data, since applications are maintained for decades
Both change on the same timescale, so no slogan is needed
Data is rewritten on every deployment, so the timescales match

questions.explanation: 'Data outlives code' is the reason schema evolution is a permanent obligation rather than a migration task.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about migrating data into a new schema, and what cheap alternative do relational databases offer?

options.text: Rewriting (migrating) data into a new schema is certainly possible, but it's an expensive thing to do on a large dataset, so most databases avoid it if possible. Most relational databases allow simple schema changes such as adding a new column with a null default value without rewriting existing data: when an old row is read, the database fills in nulls for any columns that are missing from the encoded data on disk
Migration is cheap and always performed automatically
Relational databases always rewrite the table on any schema change
Relational databases forbid adding columns after table creation

questions.explanation: Which is exactly schema-on-read behaviour, implemented inside a schema-on-write database. A footnote notes MySQL is the exception, often rewriting an entire table even though it is not strictly necessary — note the hedge 'often'.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about LinkedIn's Espresso, and what illusion does schema evolution create?

options.text: Espresso, LinkedIn's document database, uses Avro for storage, allowing it to use Avro's schema evolution rules — which allows the entire database to appear as if it was encoded with a single schema, even though the underlying storage may contain records encoded with various historical versions of the schema
Espresso uses Protocol Buffers and rewrites all records on each schema change
Espresso enforces one schema at a time, like a relational database
Espresso stores raw JSON with no schema

questions.explanation: The single-schema illusion is the practical payoff of resolution at read time.

questions.question: For archival storage, which schema is used and which formats does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Since you're copying the data anyway, you might as well encode the copy of the data consistently — even though the original may contain a mixture of schema versions from different eras — so the dump is typically encoded using the latest schema. As the data dump is written in one go and is thereafter immutable, formats such as Avro object container files are a good fit; so is an analytics-friendly column-oriented format such as Parquet
The oldest schema is used, and CSV is recommended
Each record keeps its original schema, and JSON is recommended
No schema is used; raw bytes are archived

questions.explanation: Immutability plus a single schema is what makes container files and columnar formats appropriate here.

questions.question: Define the standard client/server arrangement and the word 'service'.

options.text: When you have processes that need to communicate over a network, the most common arrangement is two roles: clients and servers. The servers expose an API over the network, and clients can connect to the servers to make requests to that API — the API exposed by the server is known as a service
Peers that both expose and consume APIs; a service is a peer
Producers and consumers connected by a broker; a service is a topic
Readers and writers sharing a database; a service is a table

questions.explanation: The web is the canonical instance: browsers make GET requests to download HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images, and POST requests to submit data, standardized through HTTP, URLs, SSL/TLS and HTML — allowing any web browser to access any website, at least in theory.

questions.question: Which other kinds of client does the chapter name, and what is the technique where a browser becomes an HTTP client?

options.text: A native app running on a mobile device or a desktop computer, and a client-side JavaScript application running inside a web browser which can use XMLHttpRequest to become an HTTP client — a technique known as Ajax. In that case the server's response is typically not HTML for displaying to a human, but data in an encoding convenient for further processing by the client-side application code, such as JSON. Although HTTP may be used as the transport protocol, the API implemented on top is application-specific
Only web browsers; Ajax refers to server-side rendering
Command-line clients; the technique is called REST
Database drivers; the technique is called RPC

questions.explanation: HTTP as transport does not make the API standard — the application-level contract still has to be agreed.

questions.question: Explain the decomposition pattern where a server is itself a client, and give both names for it.

options.text: A server can itself be a client to another service — for example a typical web app server acts as a client to a database. This approach is often used to decompose a large application into smaller services by area of functionality, such that one service makes a request to another when it requires some functionality or data from that other service. This way of building applications has traditionally been called a service-oriented architecture (SOA), more recently refined and rebranded as microservices architecture
It is called n-tier architecture, or layered architecture
It is called peer-to-peer, or mesh architecture
It is called event-driven architecture, or reactive architecture

questions.explanation: SOA and microservices name the same decomposition at different points in fashion.

questions.question: In what way are services like databases, and what is the decisive difference?

options.text: In some ways services are similar to databases: they typically allow clients to submit and query data. But while databases allow arbitrary queries using the query languages of Chapter 2, services expose an application-specific API that only allows inputs and outputs predetermined by the business logic of the service. This restriction provides a degree of encapsulation: services can impose fine-grained restrictions on what clients can and cannot do
Services allow arbitrary queries while databases restrict them
Services and databases are identical in interface, differing only in durability
Services store data while databases only compute

questions.explanation: Encapsulation is the benefit bought by giving up arbitrary querying.

questions.question: State the key design goal of a service-oriented or microservices architecture, and the conclusion the chapter draws about encoding.

options.text: To make the application easier to change and maintain by making services independently deployable and evolvable — for example each service should be owned by one team, and that team should be able to release new versions of the service frequently without having to coordinate with other teams. So we should expect old and new versions of servers and clients to be running at the same time, which means the data encoding used by servers and clients must be compatible across versions of the service API — precisely the subject of this chapter
To maximize performance through binary encodings
To minimize the number of services by consolidating teams
To enforce a single shared schema across all services

questions.explanation: Independent deployability is the goal; version coexistence is the consequence; encoding compatibility is the requirement.

questions.question: Define 'web service', explain why the name is a slight misnomer, and give the three contexts.

options.text: When HTTP is used as the underlying protocol for talking to the service, it is called a web service — a slight misnomer, because web services are not only used on the web. The three contexts: a client application running on a user's device making requests to a service over HTTP, typically over the public internet; one service making requests to another service owned by the same organization, often within the same datacenter, as part of a service-oriented or microservices architecture (software that supports this kind of use case is sometimes called middleware); and one service making requests to a service owned by a different organization, usually for data exchange between different organizations' backend systems, including public APIs such as credit card processing systems, or OAuth for shared access to user data
It means any service with a browser front-end; there are two contexts, internal and external
It means a SOAP service specifically; there is only one context
It means a RESTful service; the three contexts are GET, POST and PUT

questions.explanation: Same protocol, three quite different trust and coordination environments.

questions.question: Define REST exactly, noting what it is not.

options.text: REST is not a protocol, but rather a design philosophy that builds upon the principles of HTTP. It emphasizes simple data formats, using URLs for identifying resources, and using HTTP features for cache control, authentication and content type negotiation. An API designed according to its principles is called RESTful, and it is gaining popularity compared to SOAP, at least in the context of cross-organizational service integration, and is often associated with microservices
REST is a protocol standardized by the W3C, built on SOAP
REST is an encoding format based on JSON
REST is an RPC framework using HTTP as transport

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that even within each camp there are plenty of arguments — for example HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state) often provokes discussions; the two camps are often the subject of heated debate among their respective proponents.

questions.question: What is WSDL, and what consequences follow from it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The Web Services Description Language, which enables code generation so that a client can access a remote service using local classes and method calls — useful in statically typed programming languages, but less so in dynamically typed ones
WSDL is not designed to be human-readable, and SOAP messages are often too complex to construct manually, so users of SOAP rely heavily on tool support, code generation and IDEs

For users of programming languages not supported by SOAP vendors, integration with SOAP services is difficult; and even though SOAP and its extensions are ostensibly standardized, interoperability between different vendors' implementations often causes problems
WSDL made SOAP the dominant style for modern public APIs

questions.explanation: Although SOAP is still used in many large enterprises, it has fallen out of favor in most smaller companies. The REST camp instead uses simpler approaches with less code generation — for example OpenAPI, also known as Swagger, which can describe RESTful APIs and produce documentation.

questions.question: Match each RPC ancestor to the defect the chapter charges it with.

options.text: Enterprise JavaBeans and Java's Remote Method Invocation are limited to Java; the Distributed Component Object Model is limited to Microsoft platforms; and CORBA is excessively complex, and does not provide backward or forward compatibility
EJB is Microsoft-only; DCOM is Java-only; CORBA is too simple
All three are limited to Java
All three provide full compatibility but poor performance

questions.explanation: These are the latest incarnation of a long line of technologies that received a lot of hype but have serious problems — the chapter cites 'The Rise and Fall of CORBA'.

questions.question: When does the RPC idea date from, what does it try to do, and what is the chapter's verdict?

options.text: The remote procedure call has been around since the 1970s. The RPC model tries to make a request to a remote network service look the same as calling a function or method in your programming language, within the same process — an abstraction called location transparency. Although it seems convenient at first, the approach is fundamentally flawed: a network request is very different from a local function call
It dates from the 1990s and the chapter endorses it wholeheartedly
It dates from the 1970s and the abstraction is called protocol transparency; the chapter is neutral
It dates from 2000 and the chapter calls it the future of service communication

questions.explanation: Location transparency is the specific abstraction being criticized, citing Birrell and Nelson.

questions.question: Which differences between a network request and a local function call does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Predictability and control — a local function call is predictable and either succeeds or fails depending only on parameters under your control, whereas a network request is unpredictable: the request or response may be lost, or the remote machine may be slow or unavailable, entirely outside your control, so you have to anticipate them, for example by retrying

A third outcome — a local call returns a result, throws an exception, or never returns (infinite loop or crash); a network request has another possible outcome, returning without a result due to a timeout, in which case you simply don't know what happened and have no way of knowing whether the request got through

Retries and duplication — if requests are actually getting through and only the responses are getting lost, retrying will cause the action to be performed multiple times unless you build a mechanism for deduplication (idempotence) into the protocol

Latency and variability, pointers versus encoding, and cross-language datatype translation — local calls take about the same time to execute whereas network requests are much slower and wildly variable, from less than a millisecond to many seconds; a local call can efficiently pass references (pointers) to objects in local memory whereas all parameters must be encoded into a sequence of bytes, which is fine for primitives but quickly becomes problematic with larger objects; and an RPC framework must translate datatypes from one language into another, which can end up ugly since not all languages have the same types — recall JavaScript's problems with numbers greater than 2 to the 53rd power

questions.explanation: Six differences in total. The timeout case is discussed in detail in Chapter 8, and the datatype problem doesn't exist in a single process written in a single language.

questions.question: What conclusion does the chapter draw from the six differences, and what wry observation follows?

options.text: There's no point trying to make a remote service look too much like a local object in your programming language, because it's a fundamentally different thing. Part of the appeal of REST is that it doesn't try to hide the fact that it's a network protocol — although this doesn't seem to stop people from building RPC libraries on top of REST
RPC should be abandoned entirely; REST has solved the problem
Local and remote calls should be unified through better tooling
The differences are minor and can be ignored in a datacenter

questions.explanation: Honesty about remoteness, not abolition of RPC, is the recommendation.

questions.question: Which current RPC frameworks does the chapter name, with their encodings, and how is this generation more honest about remoteness? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Thrift and Avro come with RPC support included, gRPC is an RPC implementation using Protocol Buffers, Finagle also uses Thrift, and Rest.li uses JSON over HTTP — so RPC isn't going away

Finagle and Rest.li use futures (promises) to encapsulate asynchronous actions that may fail, which also simplify situations where you need to make requests to multiple services in parallel and combine their results
gRPC supports streams, where a call consists of not just one request and one response, but a series of requests and responses over time
Some frameworks provide service discovery — allowing a client to find out at which IP address and port number it can find a particular service

questions.explanation: Futures, streams and service discovery all acknowledge, rather than hide, the network. Service discovery is picked up again under Request Routing on page 214.

questions.question: What does custom binary RPC win, and what does REST win?

options.text: Custom RPC protocols with a binary encoding format can achieve better performance than something generic like JSON over REST. But REST is good for experimentation and debugging — you can make requests to it with a web browser or the command-line tool curl, without any code generation or software installation; it is supported by all mainstream programming languages and platforms; and there is a vast ecosystem of tools available: servers, caches, load balancers, proxies, firewalls, monitoring, debugging and testing tools. So REST seems to be the predominant style for public APIs, while the main focus of RPC frameworks is on requests between services owned by the same organization, typically within the same datacenter
REST wins on performance; RPC wins on tooling
Both are equivalent in performance and tooling
RPC is predominant for public APIs; REST for internal services

questions.explanation: Performance inside the organization, ecosystem and debuggability across it.

questions.question: For RPC the chapter makes a simplifying assumption that databases don't allow. What is it, and which compatibility do you need where?

options.text: It is reasonable to assume that all the servers will be updated first, and all the clients second. So you only need backward compatibility on requests, and forward compatibility on responses
Clients are updated first, so you need forward compatibility on requests and backward on responses
You need backward compatibility on both requests and responses
You need forward compatibility on both requests and responses

questions.explanation: Servers-first means a new server may read an old client's request (backward) and an old client may read a new server's response (forward). Getting this backwards is the classic error. For evolvability it is important that RPC clients and servers can be changed and deployed independently.

questions.question: 'The backward and forward compatibility properties of an RPC scheme are inherited from whatever encoding it uses.' Spell out the three cases. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Thrift, gRPC (Protocol Buffers) and Avro RPC can be evolved according to the compatibility rules of the respective encoding format
In SOAP, requests and responses are specified with XML schemas, which can be evolved, but there are some subtle pitfalls

RESTful APIs most commonly use JSON without a formally specified schema for responses, and JSON or URI-encoded/form-encoded request parameters for requests; adding optional request parameters and adding new fields to response objects are usually considered changes that maintain compatibility
All RPC schemes have identical compatibility properties regardless of encoding

questions.explanation: The encoding determines the rules; the RPC layer inherits them.

questions.question: What makes service compatibility harder than database compatibility?

options.text: RPC is often used for communication across organizational boundaries, so the provider of a service often has no control over its clients and cannot force them to upgrade. Thus compatibility needs to be maintained for a long time, perhaps indefinitely — and if a compatibility-breaking change is required, the service provider often ends up maintaining multiple versions of the service API side by side
Services carry more data than databases
Service protocols change faster than storage formats
Services cannot use schema registries

questions.explanation: Loss of control over the client is what makes the obligation open-ended.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about API versioning?

options.text: There is no agreement on how API versioning should work — that is, how a client can indicate which version of the API it wants to use. For RESTful APIs, common approaches are to use a version number in the URL or in the HTTP Accept header. For services that use API keys to identify a particular client, another option is to store a client's requested API version on the server and to allow this version selection to be updated through a separate administrative interface
Versioning is standardized: the version always goes in the URL
Versioning is handled automatically by HTTP content negotiation
API versioning is unnecessary if the encoding is compatible

questions.explanation: The administrative-interface approach is the one Stripe is cited for.

questions.question: Where does asynchronous message passing sit relative to RPC and databases, and what are the names for the intermediary?

options.text: Somewhere between the two: it is similar to RPC in that a client's request — usually called a message — is delivered to another process with low latency, and similar to databases in that the message is not sent via a direct network connection but goes via an intermediary which stores the message temporarily. That intermediary is called a message broker, message queue, or message-oriented middleware
Entirely on the RPC side; the intermediary is called a proxy
Entirely on the database side; the intermediary is called a log
Outside both; the intermediary is called a bus

questions.explanation: RPC expects a response as quickly as possible; the database case has one process writing encoded data and another reading it sometime in the future.

questions.question: Which advantages does a message broker have over direct RPC? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can act as a buffer if the recipient is unavailable or overloaded, and thus improve system reliability
It can automatically redeliver messages to a process that has crashed, and thus prevent messages from being lost

It avoids the sender needing to know the IP address and port number of the recipient, which is particularly useful in a cloud deployment where virtual machines often come and go; and it allows one message to be sent to several recipients
It logically decouples the sender from the recipient — the sender just publishes messages and doesn't care who consumes them

questions.explanation: Five advantages; most readers remember only buffering and decoupling.
