questions.question: How does message-passing communication differ from RPC in direction, and what does 'asynchronous' mean here?

options.text: Message-passing communication is usually one-way: a sender normally doesn't expect to receive a reply to its messages. It is possible for a process to send a response, but this would usually be done on a separate channel. The pattern is asynchronous: the sender doesn't wait for the message to be delivered, but simply sends it and then forgets about it
It is bidirectional and synchronous, unlike RPC
It is one-way but synchronous, blocking until delivery
It is identical to RPC in direction and timing

questions.explanation: Send-and-forget is what distinguishes it from a request/response call.

questions.question: Name the message brokers the chapter lists, and describe the usage model. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Message brokers used to be dominated by commercial enterprise software from TIBCO, IBM WebSphere and webMethods; more recently open source implementations such as RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS and Apache Kafka have become popular

One process sends a message to a named queue or topic, and the broker ensures that the message is delivered to one or more consumers of or subscribers to that topic; there can be many producers and many consumers on the same topic

A topic provides only one-way dataflow, but a consumer may itself publish messages to another topic, or to a reply queue that is consumed by the sender of the original message — allowing a request/response dataflow similar to RPC
Brokers enforce a particular data model, so all messages must be JSON

questions.explanation: Brokers don't enforce any particular data model — a message is just a sequence of bytes with some metadata, so you can use any encoding format. If the encoding is backward and forward compatible you have the greatest flexibility to change publishers and consumers independently. Delivery semantics vary by implementation and configuration, and Chapter 11 covers this in detail.

questions.question: Define the actor model.

options.text: A programming model for concurrency in a single process. Rather than dealing directly with threads and the associated problems of race conditions, locking and deadlock, logic is encapsulated in actors. Each actor typically represents one client or entity, may have some local state which is not shared with any other actor, and communicates with other actors by sending and receiving asynchronous messages. Message delivery is not guaranteed: in certain error scenarios messages will be lost. Since each actor processes only one message at a time it doesn't need to worry about threads, and each actor can be scheduled independently by the framework
A model where all state is shared and protected by locks
A model for distributed transactions with guaranteed delivery
A model where each thread owns one message queue with guaranteed ordering

questions.explanation: Crucially, delivery is not guaranteed even within a single process — which is what makes the distributed case less of a leap.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say location transparency works better in the actor model than in RPC?

options.text: Because the actor model already assumes that messages may be lost, even within a single process. Although latency over the network is likely higher than within the same process, there is less of a fundamental mismatch between local and remote communication when using the actor model — the same message-passing mechanism is used whether sender and recipient are on the same node or different nodes, with the message transparently encoded into a byte sequence, sent over the network, and decoded on the other side
Because actor frameworks guarantee delivery over the network
Because actors run only on a single node
Because network latency is lower than local message passing

questions.explanation: A distributed actor framework essentially integrates a message broker and the actor programming model into a single framework. But if you want to perform rolling upgrades you still have to worry about forward and backward compatibility, since messages may be sent from a node running the new version to a node running the old version, and vice versa.

questions.question: Match each actor framework to its encoding and rolling-upgrade story.

options.text: Akka uses Java's built-in serialization by default, which does not provide forward or backward compatibility, but you can replace it with something like Protocol Buffers and thus gain the ability to do rolling upgrades. Orleans uses a custom data encoding format that does not support rolling upgrade deployments — to deploy a new version you need to set up a new cluster, move traffic from the old cluster to the new one, and shut down the old one, though custom serialization plug-ins can be used. In Erlang OTP it is surprisingly hard to make changes to record schemas despite the system having many features designed for high availability, so rolling upgrades are possible but need to be planned carefully; an experimental new maps datatype, a JSON-like structure introduced in Erlang R17 in 2014, may make this easier in the future
All three use Protocol Buffers by default and support rolling upgrades
Akka uses a custom format; Orleans uses Java serialization; Erlang uses JSON
None of the three supports rolling upgrades under any configuration

questions.explanation: Note the hedges: Erlang's reputation for high availability is explicitly conceded and then set against this specific weakness, and the maps fix is only experimental and only 'may' help.

questions.question: Which benefits does the summary list for rolling upgrades? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A new version of a service is gradually deployed to a few nodes at a time, rather than deploying to all nodes simultaneously
Releases can be made without downtime, thus encouraging frequent small releases over rare big releases
Deployments are made less risky, allowing faulty releases to be detected and rolled back before they affect a large number of users
These properties are hugely beneficial for evolvability, the ease of making changes to an application

questions.explanation: During such rolling upgrades, or for various other reasons, we must assume that different nodes are running different versions of our application code — hence the need for backward compatibility (new code can read old data) and forward compatibility (old code can read new data).

questions.question: Give the summary's verdict on each of the three encoding families.

options.text: Programming language–specific encodings are restricted to a single programming language and often fail to provide forward and backward compatibility. Textual formats like JSON, XML and CSV are widespread, and their compatibility depends on how you use them; they have optional schema languages which are sometimes helpful and sometimes a hindrance, and they are somewhat vague about datatypes so you have to be careful with things like numbers and binary strings. Binary schema-driven formats like Thrift, Protocol Buffers and Avro allow compact, efficient encoding with clearly defined forward and backward compatibility semantics and are useful for documentation and code generation in statically typed languages — with the downside that data needs to be decoded before it is human-readable
All three families provide equal compatibility guarantees
Textual formats are condemned outright; binary formats have no downsides
Language-specific encodings are recommended for internal use

questions.explanation: Note the precision: family two is not condemned — its compatibility depends on how you use it.

questions.question: Restate the summary's three dataflow modes, and give the chapter's final line.

options.text: Databases, where the process writing encodes and the process reading decodes; RPC and REST APIs, where the client encodes a request, the server decodes the request and encodes a response, and the client finally decodes the response; and asynchronous message passing via message brokers or actors, where nodes communicate by sending each other messages that are encoded by the sender and decoded by the recipient. The conclusion: with a bit of care, backward/forward compatibility and rolling upgrades are quite achievable. The final line: may your application's evolution be rapid and your deployments be frequent
Storage, compute and network; the final line is about performance
Batch, stream and interactive; the final line is about correctness
Client, server and broker; the final line warns against rolling upgrades

questions.explanation: Each mode is defined by who encodes and who decodes, which is exactly the relationship compatibility governs.
